The sustained reproductive activity of females well into their teenage years underscores the importance of long-term experience in maternal care and calf survival.

Male wapiti begin antler development during their first spring, a process that is tightly linked to nutritional status and body condition. Yearling males typically grow small, unbranched spikes, while prime-aged bulls carry massive, multi-tined antlers that serve both as weapons during the rut and as visual signals of dominance. Antler growth is the fastest tissue growth known among mammals, requiring substantial mineral and protein intake over a period of approximately 120 days each year. After the autumn rut, testosterone levels drop dramatically, leading to antler mineralization, velvet shedding, and eventual casting in late winter. This annual cycle of antler growth and shedding is synchronized with photoperiod and influenced by age, nutrition, and social status. Older, dominant males in good condition generally produce the largest antlers, which provide a competitive advantage in securing and defending harems during the September through October breeding season.
